en: The Mātanga Sūtra, Volume One, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Lüyan of India and Zhi Qian during the Wu Dynasty. Chapter One:
The Chapter on Delivering the Girl of Innate Nature. Chapter One: The Chapter on Delivering the Girl of Innate Nature.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Surrounded by the bhikṣus,
he taught the Dharma at the time of dawn.
Venerable Ānanda,
having dressed and taken his bowl,
entered the city to beg for alms.
Having finished his almsround,
he returned to the Jeta Grove;
along the way, he encountered [the following].
There was a large pond where the people of the village gathered to play and congregate upon its banks.
Beside the pond was a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste,
carrying a water vessel,
who had just come to fetch water.
The Elder Ānanda went to her place and said,
"Sister, I am now thirsty and exhausted."
"I am very thirsty and must drink.
Please grant me a little water.
At that time, the daughter of the donor said:
"Venerable sir, I have nothing to begrudge.
However, I am a candāla woman. If you would accept this gift from me..."
"I fear it is not appropriate.
Ānanda said,
"Sister, my name is Śramaṇa."
His mind is impartial toward the noble and the lowly;
he perceives no difference between them,
but simply observes the act of giving as it occurs.
"It is not appropriate to remain here for long.
At that time, the woman immediately took pure water.
He gave it to Ānanda.
Having finished drinking it,
Ānanda returned to his quarters.
After he had departed,
this woman took up the physical appearance, voice, speech, and deportment of Ānanda,
and became deeply attached to them.
Her desire was fierce and intense,
and she thought to herself:
"If only I could have that departing bhikṣu as my husband."
"Is this not excellent?
He further thought:
"My mother is skilled in incantations."
"Perhaps she can be made to come and become my husband;
I shall report this matter in detail to my mother.
At that time, this woman—
Carrying the water, he returned home and went to his mother’s place,
where he spoke these words:
The bhikṣu Ānanda is a disciple of the Buddha whom I hold very dear.
"If one wishes to become his husband,
only one with the strength of a mother can accomplish this task."
"I only pray that you will have compassion and surely fulfill my wish.
The mother spoke thus to her daughter.
There are two kinds of people for whom no amount of incantations or sorcery can avail.
What are these two?
First, one who has severed desire;
second, a dead person.
"As for all others, I am able to subdue them;
but as for the śramaṇa Gautama— "
His majestic virtue was so sublime and far-reaching that King Prasenajit conceived the utmost faith and reverence.
If you know that I have escaped and have brought Ānanda here,
all those outcasts will be slaughtered.
Furthermore, Gautama, your afflictions have been exhausted,
and your followers have likewise all become free from the defilement of desire.
I have heard in the past that those who have severed birth and death should be treated with increased reverence.
"How can you, on the contrary, give rise to evil karma toward her?
Having heard this, the woman wept bitterly and said:
"If my mother does not obtain Ānanda's arrival,
I shall certainly cast off my life and body.
Even if Gautama should contravene my wish."
Furthermore, it cannot remain long in this world.
Should anyone obtain it,
their manifold aspirations will be fulfilled.
Upon hearing these words,
the mother was deeply distressed and displeased,
and she said to him:
"Do not give up your life;
I shall certainly cause Ānanda to come here.
At that time, the woman's mother—
Within his own house,
he smeared the ground with cow dung and spread white *kuśa* grass over it;
in this courtyard, [he prepared the site].
Kindle a great, fierce fire.
Recite the mantra once for each of one hundred and eight exquisite *utpala* flowers.
He would immediately cast a single stalk into the fire,
reciting these mantra words:
*Amale vimale kukuṃme samadene ye nava-thūṭe piṇḍime cayaṃte puvavali-saṭe vidyud-utte keśaṭe visamaye maraṭe samaṭe bhadrāye jaye deva.*
Whether it be a Māra,
a Gandharva, or the Fire God (Agni).
The Earth Deity,
having heard this incantation of mine as well as my sacrificial offerings.
"You should immediately order Ānanda to come here.
Having spoken these words,
the Venerable Ānanda—
His mind became utterly deluded;
unaware of his own state,
he proceeded directly to the house of a caṇḍāla.
At that time, the girl’s mother saw Ānanda approaching with serene composure from afar and said to her daughter:
"Ānanda Bhikṣu has already come near here;
you should now spread out mats and bedding."
They burned incense and scattered flowers,
making it exceedingly pure and solemn.
When the girl heard her mother’s words, she...
Filled with joy and exultation,
they adorned the halls and pavilions and prepared the precious seats.
He thoroughly cleansed and swept the area,
scattering various kinds of famous flowers.
At that time, Ānanda—
Having arrived at her house,
she was choked with sobs of grief;
shedding tears, she spoke.
How meager is my merit that I have encountered such suffering and hardship.
O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
"May you deign to show compassion, bestowing your majestic protection and mindfulness so that no harm may come.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his pure divine eye,
beheld that Ānanda had been deluded and distracted by that woman.
For the sake of protection, he then spoke this mantra:
*Sittide ajude anide*. Thereupon, the World-Honored One...
Having spoken this mantra,
he said these words:
"By means of this mantra, I..."
To bring peace and security to all sentient beings who are terrified,
and likewise to benefit and pacify those who suffer from afflictions—
should there be any sentient beings who have no place of refuge.
"I shall act as their true refuge.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
The pool of precepts is cool, pure, and stainless; It can bathe sentient beings of the heat of afflictions.
If a wise person enters this pool, The dark obstructions of ignorance are forever extinguished.
Therefore, all the worthy sages of the three periods of time Unanimously honor it upon their heads and praise it together.
"If I truly bathe in this stream, may my attendant be made to return quickly.
At that time, Ānanda,
by the Buddha's supernormal power...
Furthermore, neither the power of roots of goodness nor the spells of the caṇḍālas can achieve anything against it.
He immediately left his house and returned to the Jeta Grove.
At that time, that woman...
Seeing Ānanda returning,
he said to his mother,
"The bhikṣu has departed."
The mother said to him,
"The śramaṇa Gautama must surely do so by means of his supernatural power."
And she protects and remembers it.
For this reason, she is able to cause my mantra to be broken and destroyed.
The daughter said to her mother:
"Śramaṇa Gautama,
can the power of his divine virtue surpass that of your mother?"
The mother said to her daughter,
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses virtues that are profound and vast."
This is not something that can be matched by my own power.
Even if all sentient beings in the world were to employ every incantation and spell they possess.
If they give rise to such thoughts,
all shall be completely severed and extinguished,
leaving nothing behind forever.
Whatever they do,
nothing can obstruct them;
for this reason, [they attain such power].
One should know that his power is unsurpassed.
At that time, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
There are six phrases of mantra;
its power is preeminent,
and it is fully capable of protecting all sentient beings.
It can extinguish false paths and sever all calamities and afflictions;
you should now receive, uphold, read, and recite it to bring benefit to yourself.
They also bring peace and happiness to people—
whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs,
upāsakas, or upāsikās.
Ānanda, those who wish to benefit and bring peace to themselves and to nourish and benefit all sentient beings should all receive,
uphold, and recite this six-phrase divine mantra. Ānanda!
This mantra was proclaimed by all six past Buddhas;
now I, Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
also speak this mantra.
Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devānām-indra,
the Four Heavenly Kings, and others.
All have reverently received, upheld, read, and recited it; therefore,
you should now apply yourself to its cultivation, praise, and offering,
so that it may not be forgotten or lost.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
*yatuta antali pantali kiṃyuli tamimaheśite sarajetivipantamati dharaviśa jiri miri vanilinda yata-sabatu labhulapadi katambiraya*. The Buddha addressed Ānanda: [The mantra continues...]
If there are sentient beings who receive and uphold these six phrases of the divine mantra,
when they are about to face execution, [they shall be saved].
By the power of the mantra,
one is lightly subjected to flogging and thereby escapes.
If one were to be whipped or flogged,
by reason of this mantra,
one may be spared through reprimand.
If one were subject to censure,
by the power and majesty of this divine mantra,
one shall forever be beyond reproach or disparagement.
Tranquil and at ease, Ānanda, I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa,
whether among gods, Māras, Brahmās,
humans, or non-humans.
Even if one upholds this mantra,
one may still be afflicted and harmed;
this is excepted only in the case of fixed karma.
There was nothing that could be done about it.
Then, when the night had passed, the Caṇḍāla woman...
Having bathed his body, he put on fresh, clean garments, wore a flower garland upon his head,
and adorned himself with fragrant unguents and ornaments of gold,
silver, rings, and pendants.
Adorned with necklaces as his very body,
he walked slowly and with composure toward the city of Śrāvastī.
Having reached the city gate,
he stood waiting for Ānanda.
At dawn, Ānanda—
He entered the city to beg for alms;
when the girl saw him approaching,
she felt deep joy.
They followed after him,
never abandoning him,
whether he was advancing or halting, entering or exiting.
It constantly followed after him.
Venerable Ānanda saw this occurrence.
Filled with extreme shame and remorse,
sorrowful and displeased,
he returned and went outside the city.
Arriving at the Jeta Grove,
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
a Caṇḍāla woman has tormented and harassed me excessively."
Whether walking, standing, advancing, or halting, may we never be parted from them.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will graciously bestow his compassionate protection.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Do not grieve or be distressed.
I shall cause you to be delivered from this peril."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the woman,
"Do you intend to take Ānanda as your husband?"
The woman said,
"Gautama, it is truly as the holy teaching says.
The Buddha said:
"According to the marriage customs of good women, one must inform one's parents:
'Have you now consulted your honored elders? He replied, 'Gautama, my parents have granted me their permission.'"
Therefore, I have come here.
The Buddha said:
"If your parents have already given their permission."
"You may come in person to receive the transmission from me.
Upon hearing these words,
the girl prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew to her parents' place.
Having completed his acts of reverence,
he stood to one side and addressed his parents, saying:
I wish for Ānanda to be my husband;
I only pray that you will show me compassion and go with me.
Having personally entrusted [the child] to him,
the parents then went to where the Buddha was,
prostrated themselves at his feet, and paid homage.
Sitting to one side,
the woman said, "Gautama,
my kinsman has already arrived."
At that time, the World-Honored One asked him,
"Did you truly give your daughter to Ānanda?"
He replied,
"World-Honored One, it is truly as the holy teaching and the words of the Buddha state.
You may now return to your dwelling."
At that time, the girl's parents paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the woman, saying:
"If you wish to have the bhikṣu Ānanda as your husband,
you ought to leave the household life and adopt his appearance and attire.
She replied:
"Yes, I respectfully accept your venerable instruction. As soon as the Buddha said, "Welcome," he immediately became a śramaṇa;
his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the dharma robes were upon his body.
He then preached the Dharma for them,
instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them;
that is to say, he gave a discourse on giving.
Discourse on the precepts;
discourse on rebirth in heaven;
[the teaching that] desire is impure and that renunciation is the most excellent path of deliverance.
Furthermore, this desire is an accumulation of manifold sufferings,
its flavor being exceedingly slight.
The faults and calamities are exceedingly many;
it is like a moth that,
due to its ignorance, [flies into the flame].
They cast themselves into fierce flames to burn and harm themselves;
such is the perversion of ordinary beings.
They give rise to false attachments,
driven by craving like moths chasing a flame; therefore,
the wise abandon them and keep far away from them.
She never for a moment gave rise to thoughts of affection or delight.
When the bhikṣuṇī heard this being spoken, she...
His heart was filled with joy and gladness,
and his mind became increasingly subdued.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
Knowing that the bhikṣuṇī’s mind was supple and free from all afflictions and hindrances,
he then extensively expounded for her the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
That is to say: this is suffering;
this is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering.
"This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. At that time,
the bhikṣuṇī’s mind was suddenly and clearly resolved, and she realized the Four Noble Truths, just as a new, clean, white cloth easily takes on dye.
Immediately upon his seat,
he attained the path of Arhatship and never again regressed.
Not following the teachings of others,
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
I was formerly ignorant and intoxicated by the desire for wine.
They disturb the worthy and noble ones and create unwholesome karma.
We only pray that the World-Honored One [will act accordingly].
"Accept my confession.
The Buddha said,
"I have already accepted your confession."
"You should now know that a Buddha appears in the world rarely,
and a human body is difficult to obtain."
To be liberated from birth and death and attain arhatship is likewise exceedingly difficult;
such a feat is truly hard to achieve.
You have already attained it;
within the Buddha-dharma,
you have obtained the fruit of reality.
That is to say: birth and death are exhausted;
the holy life has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished.
There will be no further existence for you.
Therefore, you should now apply yourself with diligence;
be careful not to be negligent.
Chapter Two: Clarifying Past Causes, from the *Mātanga-sūtra*.
At that time, the various brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders within the city...
When they heard that the Buddha had delivered a Caṇḍāla woman,
allowing her to leave the household life to practice the Way,
they all gave rise to feelings of resentment and indignation.
And he spoke these words:
"How can this person of lowly birth be allowed to associate with the fourfold assembly?"
We practice the holy life together.
How then should we enter the homes of the wealthy and noble to receive offerings?
In this manner, they passed the matter along from one to another until it reached the ears of King Prasenajit.
Having heard this, the king was utterly astonished;
he immediately prepared his carriage.
Surrounded by his retinue and preceded and followed by attendants, he proceeded to the Jeta Grove;
there he alighted from his carriage and removed his parasol.
He proceeded forward with a slow gait,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude and wishing to resolve their doubts,
addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to hear the past karmic conditions of the bhikṣuṇī Prakṛti?
The bhikṣus replied, "Yes, indeed;
we wish to hear them."
Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you.
Monks, in the distant past, incalculable eons ago...
On the banks of the Ganges there was a garden named Atimuktaka,
where flowers and fruits grew in profusion.
It was complete with ponds and flowing streams.
Within the garden there was a king named Tiṣya.
He is of the Caṇḍāla-Mātanga caste,
and dwells together with a multitude of hundreds of thousands of Caṇḍālas in this garden.
"O bhikṣus, that Tiṣya possessed great wisdom, was of eminent talent,
and was courageous and resolute."
They naturally remember their past lives;
there is no worldly matter with which they are not thoroughly proficient.
I shall briefly explain its five merits.
First, one will be extensively trained in the four Vedas and the essentials of their secret teachings,
such that there is nothing one does not thoroughly master.
Second, he is skilled in understanding the poems, books, prose, verses, and the long and short syllables of words.
Third, he fully knows all treatises, classics, measurements, and has reached the further shore of phonology.
Fourth, he is able to understand worldly sacrificial rites, incantations, arts, and medicine.
The five excellent analytical marks of a great man—
such wisdom is inexhaustible.
That king had a son named Siṃhakarṇa,
whose countenance was upright and handsome.
Their conduct in the precepts is pure;
their minds are disciplined and gentle;
they are benevolent, kind, and harmonious.
Possessing all virtues and worthy of universal veneration,
those who see him rejoice;
he is King Mātanga.
He extensively instructed his son in all the scriptures, incantations,
and arts that he himself knew.
He instructed them all thoroughly;
therefore, Siṃhakarṇa’s knowledge and vision were profound and far-reaching.
He was also just like his father;
they were equal and no different. King Diśāṃpati.
While lying down at night,
the thought suddenly arose in him:
"As for my son's appearance..."
It is most preeminent,
endowed with all virtues,
and revered by all people.
As he gradually grew older,
it was appropriate to betroth him a wife;
one must certainly select a beautiful and virtuous match.
Only when one's talent and virtue are preeminent, such as those of your son,
shall I then seek a wife for him on your behalf.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Padmagarbha.
The clan is noble and distinguished;
the parents are of pure lineage,
tracing back seven generations.
Pure and without blemish,
he was proficient in the four Vedas,
and his talents were rarely equaled.
At that time, there was a king named Mahāvyuha who ruled over the entire world.
Possessing sovereign power,
he granted a single village as a fief,
sealed with a lotus seed.
He was appointed as its ruler;
that land became prosperous and its people were wealthy and numerous.
That daughter of the Lotus-fruit,
named Prakṛti,
was preeminent in virtue and appearance.
It was like the ears of a lion.
King Diśāṃpati thought to himself:
"Only the lotus fruit remains;
that daughter is most exquisite.
I shall seek her hand for you as a wife."
Having formed this thought,
at dawn on the following morning,
he mounted a great precious chariot.
He was mounted on a carriage drawn by four white horses,
surrounded before and behind by a multitude of caṇḍālas.
Having left the household life,
he traveled north toward that country,
which lay to the south of where Padmagarbha resided.
There was a garden called Nandana,
where flowers and fruits flourished in abundance.
The trees flourish and bloom;
springs and bathing pools are filled with pure water.
Various species of birds sported upon it,
their plaintive songs harmonizing with one another.
Those who hear this are filled with joy;
that garden is vast and expansive,
exceedingly delightful.
It was like the Nandana Garden of the devas;
King Mātanga went into that garden.
While waiting for the lotus seeds to ripen,
at that time, the brahmin also rose in the early morning.
He was mounted upon a carriage drawn by four white horses,
accompanied by five hundred Brahmins,
all of whom escorted and surrounded him.
Upon arriving at the park for recreation,
that brahmin was by the side of the road.
Having instructed his disciples in the arts and other matters,
and having first practiced his recitations,
he came to the garden.
King Diśāṃpati saw the lotus fruit and approached with composure.
His majestic virtue was extraordinary;
his heart gave rise to joy,
and he praised him in verse, saying:
Just as when the sun first rises, its radiance shines brightly, so too is the majestic power of the Great Being.
Like the medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains, which are the most excellent among all medicines, the Benevolent One is lofty and far-reaching;
there is nothing that can compare to him, for his virtuous power is profound and wondrous.
Extremely majestic and radiant, like the autumn moon;
among all the stars, he is like the Brahmā King. His wisdom is preeminent and surpassing;
he is gazed upon by all the devas, like Śakra, Lord of Devas, whom all revere with respect.
Your majestic beauty is peerless, beyond all comparison;
I have merely briefly praised your virtues, for were they to be explained in detail, they would be inexhaustible.
Having spoken this verse, [he continued:]
He immediately rose to welcome him.
They exchanged greetings with one another,
and then took their seats.
The Lotus Real Mantra said:
"You, O Caṇḍāla, most base and inferior, have come here."
"What do you wish to do?
He replied,
"Noble sir, there are four matters in the world."
One should practice these.
What are the four?
First, the original purpose for which one acts.
First, to remember and not forget;
second, to bring benefit and peace to oneself;
third, to benefit all sentient beings.
Fourth, we are intent on arranging a marriage alliance;
for this reason, I have now come to visit you. I have a son.
His name was Siṃhakarṇa.
His countenance was magnificent and his wisdom was subtle and profound.
I wish to betroth a wife to you;
your virtuous daughter is most excellent,
and my heart is deeply enamored with her.
I wish to entrust my daughter to you in marriage;
I hope you will deign to consider this and grant your consent.
At that time, having heard these words,
Padmagarbha’s poisonous anger blazed up intensely.
He gave rise to extreme anger;
his countenance became grim and constrained,
and his features were knit into a frown.
And he said to him:
"The Mātanga caste is held in contempt by all people."
It is utterly loathsome and evil,
like poison and like fire.
My present body belongs to the Brahmin caste.
He was preeminent and most noble;
there was none who surpassed him,
and he had mastered the Vedas.
Your wisdom is peerless;
how can you now wish to come and bring me disgrace?
It would be like comparing the light of the moon in the sky to that of a firefly or a candle.
Those with eyes all recognize this as extraordinary;
he is of the Caṇḍāla caste.
The distinction between the noble and the base among brahmins is likewise the same.
Now you are foolish;
not recognizing that which is noble or base, nor that which is unattainable,
you have conceived a mind of longing.
"You, O Caṇḍāla,
belong to your own kind;
why do you desire to defile those who are pure and superior?"
Furthermore, O Brahmin,
your ethical conduct is incomplete,
and you have not mastered the sublime scriptures of the Vedas.
The various brahmins do not associate with him;
how much less would they do so with you,
a common and lowly person, that you should even conceive such a thought.
"You must depart quickly;
you should not remain for long. Do not let outsiders hear these extraordinary words.
At that time, Di Shengjia—
Having heard this matter,
he said: "O worthy one,
gold, jade, and rare treasures— "
He fully knows all things, from the decay and defects of earthworks to the differing appearances of the noble and the lowly.
I now see no difference between these brahmins and the candālas.
For what reason? You, O Brahmin, did not emerge from space;
the Caṇḍāla caste alone was born from the earth.
As for the Brahmins—
Born from a womb,
the Cāṇḍāla caste is likewise the same.
To claim that it is superior is impossible;
for the Brahmin has died.
Hated and loathed by people,
even when a candāla dies,
no one wishes to see him.
If you say that there are distinctions based on noble and base status,
why then is there no difference between birth and death?
This is what you must consider.
A candāla is one who commits evil deeds,
being fierce, violent, and cruel.
They deceive sentient beings and lack a heart of compassion;
for these reasons, [they fall into hell].
"You are called base and lowly.
I shall now declare to you, O brāhmaṇa,
all your evil deeds and false matters."
They give rise to disputes and litigation,
disturb and confound the virtuous and good,
and create demonic portents.
They practice astrology and observe the moon;
they arrange military formations and slaughter sentient beings.
To state the essentials:
all evil deeds are the work of the Brahmins.
"O Brahmin, you who by nature delight in fine flavors,
yet you speak these words."
If one performs a sacrificial offering,
one may recite incantations over a sheep and slaughter it;
the sheep will certainly be reborn in heaven.
If reciting mantras can cause one to be reborn in heaven,
why do you not now recite them over your own body and kill it as an offering to seek rebirth in heaven?
Why do you not recite them over your parents, friends, wife, children, and kinsmen?
He slaughters them all to cause them to be born in heaven,
rather than extinguishing his own body.
One should know that those who slaughter sheep are all Brahmins,
acting out of a desire to eat meat.
To falsely make such a claim is the act of a deceptive person who speaks of himself as being honored and superior.
This is logically untenable.
According to the Dharma of the Brahmins,
there are four kinds of offenses.
They are called extremely evil and are not true Brahmins.
What are these four?
First, killing a brahmin;
second, committing adultery with one's teacher's wife;
third, stealing gold.
The fourth is drinking alcohol.
These four evils alone are designated as transgressions.
As for all other acts of killing,
they have no retribution at all;
yet in your own dharma...
One incurs the sin of killing by taking the life of another;
this applies even if one kills someone other than [the intended victim].
It is also called taking life.
Why is it that killing [them] alone incurs no sin?
Even regarding the drinking of alcohol,
it is likewise so.
You should know that you all are foolish and devoid of wisdom.
They give rise to perverse delusions;
one cannot call this being noble or eminent.
Furthermore, O Brahmin:
If one commits the first four offenses,
by repenting with a sincere heart,
they may still be extinguished.
Holding the leg of a bed in his hand,
wearing tattered and ruined garments,
and [carrying] a human skull.
He hung his head above [the ground] and performed repentance in this manner for a full twelve years.
Their precepts are fully restored,
and they become brahmins;
such is their foolishness.
Following after false views,
they give rise to arrogance and pride,
claiming themselves to be honorable and noble.
Viewed from this perspective,
all lineages are equal; therefore,
you may grant your virtuous daughter to my son.
When Padmagarbha heard these words,
his anger increased all the more.
"Devadatta, you have spoken these words recklessly, without having reflected upon them."
As you are a king,
you should know three dharmas:
first, the dharma of the realm.
Second, the laws concerning nobility and commoners;
third, the laws concerning tribute and taxation.
